cases.title: The box that rebuilt world trade

skeleton.brief: Shipping costs plummeted from $5.80 to 16 cents per ton
Cargo moved as break bulk, slow and inefficient
Malcolm McLean's 1956 Ideal X container ship voyage
1960s debates on container size and ISO standardization
Vietnam War drove container adoption with military logistics
Ports relocated to accommodate container cranes and yards
800 million container moves yearly enable global manufacturing

narration.text: In 1956 loading a ship cost about five dollars and eighty cents a ton. Within a decade the same ton cost sixteen cents.
Before containerization, cargo moved as break bulk: sacks, crates, and barrels, each handled by gangs of dockworkers and stacked by eye. A ship could spend longer in port than at sea.

asset_request.description: dockworkers loading sacks and crates manually on a ship
asset_request.guidance: A daylight photo of dockworkers handling various sacks and crates on a ship dock, showing manual labor and cargo stacking.

slot_banner.heading: Break Bulk Cargo: Slow and Inefficient

narration.text: Malcolm McLean was a trucking man who revolutionized shipping. In April 1956, he loaded fifty-eight aluminium truck bodies onto the Ideal X, a converted tanker, and sailed them from Newark to Houston.

The 1960s were spent debating container sizes. Ports, railways, and truckers all wanted different boxes. The ISO standard fixed corner castings and set twenty and forty foot lengths between 1968 and 1970.

asset_request.description: containers of different sizes stacked at a port with cranes
asset_request.guidance: A clear photo showing various container sizes stacked at a busy port with cranes in the background.

slot_panel.heading: Container Size Standardization
bullets: Ports, railways, and truckers debated sizes

narration.text: The Vietnam War made container shipping essential. The US military needed reliable resupply across the Pacific. Containers paid for ships and cranes later used by civilian trade.

asset_request.description: US military cargo containers being loaded onto a ship
asset_request.guidance: A photo of military containers being loaded onto a ship, showing military logistics in action.

asset_request.description: container cranes at a busy port
asset_request.guidance: A wide shot of container cranes operating at a busy commercial port.

asset_request.description: cargo ship sailing with containers
asset_request.guidance: A photo of a container ship sailing on the ocean loaded with containers.

narration.text: Ports relocated to accommodate container cranes and yards. New York’s Manhattan piers were replaced by Newark across the harbor, a story repeated in London, Liverpool, and San Francisco.
Today, around eight hundred million container movements happen each year. The container box didn’t just cut costs; it made manufacturing across the globe possible.

cases.title: How penicillin actually got made

skeleton.brief: Fleming's mould discovery is famous but underexplained
Fleming finds bacteria-killing mould in 1928 but can't extract penicillin
Oxford team revives penicillin research in 1939 with makeshift extraction
First patient treated in 1941 improves then dies as supply runs out
Florey seeks US help due to wartime British production limits
US lab boosts yield using corn steep liquor and mouldy cantaloupe
By D-Day 1944, penicillin supply meets Allied soldiers' needs
Fleming, Florey, Chain win Nobel Prize in 1945 for penicillin

narration.text: Alexander Fleming noticed a mould killing bacteria on a forgotten petri dish in 1928, but then largely put it down.

slot_quote.heading: "The discovery of penicillin was a chance observation."

narration.text: In 1928, Fleming found bacteria-killing mould in his London lab but couldn't extract penicillin effectively.
In 1939, the Oxford team led by Florey, Chain, and Heatley revived penicillin research. Heatley built an extraction rig from bedpans, milk churns, and even a doorbell to isolate the drug.

narration.text: The first patient treated in 1941, Albert Alexander, improved but died when the penicillin supply ran out. They even recovered the drug from his urine to continue treatment.
With Britain under bombing and limited production, Florey traveled to the United States to seek help for penicillin manufacturing.
A US lab in Peoria boosted penicillin yield using corn steep liquor and a mouldy cantaloupe from a local market, which carried the industrial strain.

cases.title: The water cycle, properly

skeleton.brief: Introduce the common circular water cycle drawing
Explain evaporation mostly from oceans
Describe condensation forming clouds around dust and salt
Show precipitation imbalance favoring ocean return
Detail water splitting on land into runoff, soil, groundwater
Explain collection back to ocean completing the cycle
Highlight cycle duration varies from days to thousands of years

narration.text: Every school draws the water cycle as a circle, and the circle is right.

slot_stat.heading: The water cycle is a circle
bullets: But the drawing leaves out how uneven each step is

narration.text: Start with evaporation. About eighty-six percent of the water that enters the atmosphere comes off the ocean, not off lakes and rivers.

asset_request.description: ocean surface with evaporation
asset_request.guidance: A clear shot of ocean water with visible evaporation or mist rising, avoid boats or people.

slot_panel.heading: Evaporation mostly from oceans
bullets: 86% of atmospheric water vapor comes from oceans
Lakes and rivers contribute much less

narration.text: That vapour rises, cools and condenses into cloud droplets around specks of dust and salt. Without those specks the air would just stay humid.

asset_request.description: diagram of cloud droplets forming around dust and salt particles
asset_request.guidance: A clear, simple diagram showing cloud droplets forming around dust and salt particles on a plain background, no text.

narration.text: Then precipitation, and here is the imbalance: about seventy-eight percent of rain falls back onto the ocean it came from. Only the remainder reaches land at all.
On land the water splits three ways. Some runs off into rivers, some soaks into the soil for plants, and some sinks into groundwater that may not see the surface for a thousand years.

asset_request.description: river runoff, soil moisture, and groundwater infiltration
asset_request.guidance: Three distinct images showing river runoff, soil moisture with plants, and groundwater infiltration, avoid text overlays.

slot_right.heading: Water splits on land
bullets: Sinks into groundwater lasting up to 1000 years

narration.text: And then collection, back to the ocean, and the loop starts again.
The cycle takes about nine days for a single molecule in the atmosphere, and up to ten thousand years for one that ends up in deep groundwater. Same loop, wildly different speeds.

slot_main.heading: Cycle duration varies wildly
bullets: About 9 days for atmospheric water molecules
Up to 10,000 years in deep groundwater

skeleton.brief: Boarding passes look simple but hide secret functions

slot_custom.heading: Inside a boarding pass

narration.text: Top left is the passenger name, printed exactly as it appears in the reservation system, which is why a middle initial can matter at the gate.
The flight number carries the airline's two letter code and up to four digits. Even numbers usually mean eastbound or northbound, odd numbers the return leg.
The seat is obvious. The letter beside it is not: the boarding group, which is set by fare class and status, and is the only field on the card that decides what happens to your bag.
Then there is a short string in the corner that most people never notice, something like S or SSSS. Four S characters means secondary screening was selected before you ever reached the airport.

slot_myth_fact.myth: The screening codes are random or meaningless.
slot_myth_fact.fact: Four S characters mean you were selected for secondary screening before arriving at the airport.
slot_myth_fact.heading: Screening codes explained

narration.text: And the barcode at the bottom is not encrypted. It carries your name, your record locator and your frequent flyer number in plain text, which is why photographing your pass for social media is a genuinely bad idea.
Every one of those fields was added because something went wrong once.

cases.title: The five layers of the atmosphere

skeleton.brief: Atmosphere is not a fog but five distinct layers
Temperature changes define atmospheric layers
Troposphere: weather layer, temperature falls with height
Stratosphere: temperature rises due to ozone absorption
Mesosphere: coldest layer where meteors burn up
Thermosphere: very hot but thin, aurora and space station
Exosphere: outer fade-out, atoms drift into space
Five layers separated by temperature shifts

narration.text: The atmosphere is not a fog that thins out. It is five distinct layers.

asset_request.description: layers of Earth's atmosphere visualized in sky
asset_request.guidance: A clear image showing distinct layers of Earth's atmosphere with color gradients, no text overlays.

slot_banner.heading: The atmosphere has five distinct layers

narration.text: What separates these layers is whether the temperature rises or falls as you climb higher. Temperature changes define each atmospheric layer.
The troposphere is the bottom twelve kilometres where all the weather happens. Here, the temperature falls the higher you go. Everything you've seen in the sky occurs in this layer.

asset_request.description: stormy weather with clouds and rain
asset_request.guidance: A dynamic photo of storm clouds and rain showing weather activity in the troposphere.

narration.text: Above the troposphere is the stratosphere, reaching about fifty kilometres. Here, temperature rises because the ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet light. This warm-on-top setup prevents mixing and allows airliners to fly safely at its bottom.

asset_request.description: airliner flying high with clear sky
asset_request.guidance: A clear photo of a commercial airplane flying high in the stratosphere with blue sky background.

narration.text: The mesosphere extends to about eighty-five kilometres and is the coldest layer, around minus ninety degrees. Meteors burn up here as they enter Earth's atmosphere.

asset_request.description: meteor burning up in night sky
asset_request.guidance: A clear night photo showing a bright meteor burning up in the mesosphere.

narration.text: The thermosphere stretches up to six hundred kilometres. Though temperatures can reach thousands of degrees, the air is so thin a thermometer would feel cold. This is where auroras occur and where the space station orbits.

asset_request.description: aurora borealis with space station overhead
asset_request.guidance: A vivid photo of aurora borealis with the International Space Station visible above.

slot_right.heading: Thermosphere: Hot but Thin
bullets: Auroras and space station orbit here

narration.text: The exosphere is the outermost layer where hydrogen and helium atoms slowly drift off into space. It is a gradual fade-out from our atmosphere into the vacuum beyond.

asset_request.description: space fade out with Earth horizon
asset_request.guidance: A photo showing Earth's horizon fading into space with stars and darkness beyond.

narration.text: To sum up, the five layers of the atmosphere are separated by boundaries where the temperature changes direction, rising or falling as you go higher.

pros: Important for weather, aviation, and space
